title: The One With The Blackout

jokes.text: Phoebe introduces a song about 'what life is really all about' and plays approximately two notes before the power cuts out
jokes.setup: Phoebe builds anticipation for a meaningful, profound song about life's deepest meaning
jokes.punchline: The blackout hits immediately, cutting her off after a few seconds — the universe itself cancels her performance
jokes.explanation: The cold open is a tight, well-structured comedic premise. The setup is patient — Phoebe's earnest, grandiose intro ('what life is really all about') primes us for something either profound or ridiculous, and the instant blackout delivers pure comic deflation. The character integration is excellent: only Phoebe would frame a Central Perk set this pretentiously. The structure earns its score because the timing is mechanical perfection — the punchline is the episode title card itself.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: when you suddenly realize what life is really all about

jokes.text: Monica on the phone with her mom: 'Pants and a sweater. Why, Mom?'
jokes.setup: Monica is excited about the blackout romance possibilities; her mother calls and immediately starts mothering her about clothing
jokes.punchline: Monica's exasperated 'Pants and a sweater. Why, Mom?' reveals her mom is already giving her unsolicited fashion advice in a crisis
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient character joke. Monica's controlling mother is an established character type, and this is a small but well-placed beat — the mom's first instinct during a citywide blackout is to tell her daughter what to wear. Competent and funny, but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what if I meet someone during the blackout?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, it's a blackout, not a singles event.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, but what if there's eligible looters out there?

jokes.text: Monica: 'Who will I meet in a blackout? Power-company guys? Eligible looters?'
jokes.setup: Monica immediately pivots from the citywide emergency to thinking about meeting men
jokes.punchline: Her list of potential romantic prospects peaks absurdly at 'eligible looters'
jokes.explanation: Sharp character work. Monica's romantic desperation is a core trait, and pivoting from 'power-company guys' (plausible) to 'eligible looters' (absurd qualifier) is a clean escalating joke. The word 'eligible' doing heavy lifting to make a criminal class sound like a dating pool is genuinely clever economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't know my own phone number.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I've never called myself.

jokes.text: Joey tries to call his own apartment to check on his grandma: 'What's my number? I never call me.'
jokes.setup: Joey asks to borrow the phone to check on his grandma during the blackout
jokes.punchline: He doesn't know his own phone number because he has never had reason to call himself
jokes.explanation: A beautifully simple Joey joke. 'I never call me' is the kind of self-evident but absurd logic that is Joey's comedic signature — he's not dumb, he's just operating by his own internally consistent rules. The economy is excellent: two short sentences reveal everything about the character. High character integration score because this joke only works for Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God! That's... that's Janice Litman! I mean, no, wait—that's the supermodel! From the... from the thing! The thing in the magazine!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, is this a vestibule or an atrium? Because I've been saying vestibule, but what if it's actually an atrium? She probably knows. Models know about architecture, right? Or do they? Why am I thinking about this right now?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Focus, Chandler. She's right there. Just be cool. Don't say anything stupid. Although, technically, is this space a vestibule or an atrium? Because Joey said it was a vestibule, but Monica thought—no, no, focus on the supermodel!

jokes.text: Chandler's internal monologue: 'I am trapped in an ATM vestibule with Jill Goodacre.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is stuck at the bank during the blackout with a Victoria's Secret model
jokes.punchline: He narrates his situation to himself with the reverence of a man witnessing a miracle, framing a random inconvenience as the greatest moment of his life
jokes.explanation: A solid setup line that establishes the episode's B-plot comedic premise. Chandler's wide-eyed awe is well-rendered. The repetition of this phrase across the episode builds the joke; this first instance is good but gains value as a callback anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could you just... I mean, would you mind if I... look, I'm trapped here with you, and you're gorgeous, and I'm trying to focus, but you keep using words like 'buttress' and 'corbel'...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, no, that's not what I meant. Could we maybe talk about something else? Anything? Like... load-bearing walls? No, that's still architecture. My brain is a terrible, terrible place.

jokes.text: Chandler internally second-guesses: 'Is it a vestibule? Maybe it's an atrium.' Then: 'Yeah, that is the part to focus on, you idiot.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is starstruck next to a supermodel and narrating his own experience
jokes.punchline: Rather than focusing on the extraordinary moment, he gets anxious about the correct architectural term and then immediately calls himself an idiot for it
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes and a defining Chandler moment. The specificity of the joke is exceptional: instead of being paralyzed by nerves or lust like a normal person, Chandler's anxiety manifests as an obsessive need to correctly categorize the room he's standing in. This is precisely Chandler's brand of deflective, neurotic humor — his defense mechanism is pedantry. The self-aware follow-up ('that is the part to focus on, you idiot') closes the loop perfectly. High character integration because no other Friend would make this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I am some guy

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Jill says vestibule, I'm going with vestibule.'
jokes.setup: Chandler just had an internal debate about 'vestibule' vs. 'atrium'
jokes.punchline: He resolves his architectural anxiety by simply deferring to whatever the supermodel says, abandoning all pretense of independent thought
jokes.explanation: A tight callback that pays off the previous joke economically. The comedy is in how quickly Chandler abandons his pedantic principle: a second ago he wanted the correct term; now he'll accept any term as long as Jill Goodacre used it. It's a clean two-beat joke about male starstruck servility. 'Jill says vestibule, I'm going with vestibule' is genuinely quotable as a standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm Rabbi Tribbiani.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, look at all those candles in Ugly Naked Guy's apartment!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's a fire hazard.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, that had to hurt.

jokes.text: Jill tells her friend on the phone she's 'not alone' — 'I don't know, some guy.' Chandler reacts: 'Oh, some guy. I am some guy.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is internally convinced this is a mythic moment; Jill dismisses him as 'some guy' to her friend
jokes.punchline: The gap between Chandler's self-mythologizing and Jill's complete indifference — 'I am some guy' — is the punchline
jokes.explanation: A solid deflation joke. The irony of Chandler treating this encounter as life-defining while Jill can't even categorize him is clean and relatable. The understated delivery of 'I am some guy' works because Chandler is internalizing the humiliation in real-time. Good structure, decent impact.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So... nice weather we're having.

dialogue.speaker: Jill
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: *smiles widely*

dialogue.speaker: Jill
dialogue.line: *looks away nervously*

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm just gonna keep smiling. Women love that, right?

dialogue.speaker: Jill
dialogue.line: Actually, no. You're scaring me.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: *smile gets bigger* See? It's working!

jokes.text: Ross enters with candles: 'Officiating at tonight's blackout is Rabbi Tribbiani. Chandler's old roommate was Jewish. These are our only candles. So happy Hanukkah!'
jokes.setup: The group needs candles for the blackout; Ross arrives with candles and a makeshift rationale
jokes.punchline: The logic chain — 'we need candles → Hanukkah candles → Chandler's roommate was Jewish → therefore Rabbi Tribbiani officiates Hanukkah' — is absurd and delivered with complete conviction
jokes.explanation: A mildly funny bit of absurdist logic. The 'Rabbi Tribbiani' construction is funny because of the incongruity of Joey's Italian surname with the Hanukkah context. The joke is stretched a bit thin across multiple sentences but lands adequately.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: If you ever need anything, just call me. I'll come running.

dialogue.speaker: Jill
dialogue.line: That's so sweet. You know, I had 300 romantic options in high school.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? Well, I had a peanut allergy and severe anxiety.

jokes.text: 'Look! Ugly Naked Guy lit a bunch of candles.' [beat] 'That had to hurt!'
jokes.setup: The group is observing the blacked-out city; someone spots Ugly Naked Guy across the way
jokes.punchline: The candles illuminating Ugly Naked Guy presumably reveal something about where he's placed them, prompting 'That had to hurt!'
jokes.explanation: A well-timed visual gag that uses the show's established running character (Ugly Naked Guy) for a quick dark innuendo. The economy is strong — 'that had to hurt' does all the work. The audience fills in the visual, which is funnier than showing it. The running-gag status of Ugly Naked Guy gives it bonus familiarity points.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, Monica! I have the most amazing news!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Mmph mrph mrmph mrmph!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Mmph mrph mrmph mrmph mrmph!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, I can't understand you!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, oh! I got it. He said he's getting married!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, what?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes! I'm proposing to Monica!

jokes.text: Chandler's internal pep talk: 'All right, it's been 14 and a half minutes and you still haven't said one word. God! Do something! Just make contact. Smile!'
jokes.setup: Chandler has been silently standing next to Jill Goodacre for nearly 15 minutes without speaking
jokes.punchline: His internal monologue is a frantic self-coaching session that reveals the depth of his social paralysis
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy establishing the depth of Chandler's dysfunction. The specificity of '14 and a half minutes' is a nice touch. Mostly setup-work for the smile beat that follows, so the laughs are moderate on their own.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So there I was, on this pool table...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's my sister!

jokes.text: Chandler finally smiles at Jill — and the smile is clearly terrifying. Chandler's internal voice: 'You're definitely scaring her.'
jokes.setup: Chandler psychs himself up to make contact — just smile!
jokes.punchline: The smile he produces is apparently so unnerving that he immediately diagnoses it as frightening
jokes.explanation: A strong visual gag that relies on the performance. The setup is clean (just smile!) and the payoff — the smile is worse than silence — is a satisfying inversion. Chandler's self-aware 'you're definitely scaring her' is the perfect deadpan close. High rewatch value because the physical performance sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So I did it in a movie theater.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, it was crazy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, where's the weirdest place you've ever done it?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Milwaukee.

jokes.text: Chandler's mom calls; she's 'tripping' because 'the blackout's scaring the dog, Dexter.' Chandler: 'You'd pee in Dad's shoes too if you didn't know.'
jokes.setup: Chandler's mom is panicking about the dog's behavior during the blackout
jokes.punchline: Chandler's empathetic defense of the dog — 'you'd pee in Dad's shoes too if you didn't know' — casually implies dark things about his father
jokes.explanation: A decent Chandler family-dysfunction joke. The implication that the dog peeing in Dad's shoes is understandable, even justified, is a nice dark touch. It's not a standout but it's characteristic and functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So there was this broken ride, right? And I may have... gotten a little too close to it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And when security started looking for me, I may have hidden behind the mechanical Dutch children in It's a Small World.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Which is why I'm permanently banned from Disney.

jokes.text: Chandler gets a word in with Jill — 'Mothers.' She says 'Yeah.' His internal voice: 'Attaboy! A word. That wasn't so hard. Mothers. Yeah! Perfect.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has been unable to speak for 15 minutes; he finally manages to say one word
jokes.punchline: His internal celebration of saying a single word ('Mothers') is wildly disproportionate to the achievement
jokes.explanation: A well-executed cringe payoff. The escalating internal triumph ('Attaboy! A word. That wasn't so hard... Perfect!') is funny because the achievement is so minimal. The joke works because we've been suffering through Chandler's paralysis with him, so the release valve is earned.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: The weirdest place? The foot of the bed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The foot of the bed?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not weird, that's where feet go.

jokes.text: Jill offers Chandler the phone: 'Would you like to call somebody?' Chandler internally: 'Yeah, about 300 guys I went to high school with.'
jokes.setup: Jill politely offers her phone to Chandler
jokes.punchline: Chandler's first instinct is to call every guy from his past who would be devastated with envy — the call is about bragging, not connection
jokes.explanation: A sharp, compact joke that reveals Chandler's social insecurity through a very specific fantasy. '300 guys from high school' implies both that he had a large social circle and that his primary joy would be making them jealous. Good economy and strong character insight.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And you didn't marry him because...?

jokes.text: Chandler calls the apartment and tells Ross he's stuck in 'an ATM vestibule with Jill Goodacre' — Ross can't hear him and hands the phone to Joey, who immediately understands and screams: 'Oh my God! He's trapped in an ATM vestibule with Jill Goodacre!'
jokes.setup: Chandler calls to share the news; Ross can't understand the whispered message and hands off to Joey
jokes.punchline: Joey not only immediately comprehends (unlike the more intellectual Ross) but amplifies the announcement to the whole room
jokes.explanation: Strong three-character bit. The joke has two layers: first, Ross's bafflement (the 'intellectual' can't decode a simple message), then Joey's instant comprehension and broadcast of it to the apartment — which is the opposite of what Chandler needed. The character inversion (Joey getting it, Ross not) is good writing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know, in a long-term relationship, passion fades and gets replaced by other things.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Like, in my case, my ex-wife became a lesbian.

jokes.text: Joey gives Chandler phone advice through the call; Chandler says: 'Like that thought never entered my mind.'
jokes.setup: Joey is coaching Chandler on what to do with the supermodel (presumably to ask her out or make a move)
jokes.punchline: Chandler's sarcastic response implies Joey's 'advice' is painfully obvious — of course he'd already thought of it
jokes.explanation: A routine sarcastic retort. Functional but not distinctive. The joke is predictable — of course Chandler has already thought about making a move.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know, Ross, you're really... you're really something special.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Ah. It's never gonna happen.

jokes.text: The group plays 'weirdest place you've had sex.' Monica: 'Senior year of college, on a pool table.' Joey: 'Pool table? That's my sister.'
jokes.setup: Monica reveals she had sex on a pool table in college
jokes.punchline: Joey's response isn't jealousy or judgment — it's the realization that the story overlaps with his sister's experience
jokes.explanation: A genuinely well-constructed joke. The setup is Monica being casually scandalous; the punchline is Joey's reaction, which reframes the story entirely — not as a Monica anecdote but as a Tribbiani family scandal. 'That's my sister' is delivered with the precise level of dawning horror. The economy is near-perfect: two words do all the work. Strong character integration for Joey specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're in the friend zone, Ross. You need to make a move.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm laying groundwork. It's all part of my strategy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're not laying groundwork. You're the mayor of the Zone.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not fair.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Not only are you the mayor, you're the governor. You're the whole government. Pretty soon you'll be taking a vow of celibacy and joining the priesthood.

jokes.text: Chandler's weirdest place: 'the women's room of the New York City Public Library.' Ross responds: 'Oh my God! What were you doing in a library?'
jokes.setup: Chandler reveals an impressively scandalous 'weirdest place' answer
jokes.punchline: Ross's response ignores the sex part entirely and focuses on the library — as if that's the more surprising element
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup (Chandler's scandalous answer) primes the room for a response about the sex; Ross's misdirection to 'what were you doing in a library?' is a perfect inversion. It works on multiple levels: it's a genuinely great misdirection joke, it's perfectly in character for Ross (bookish, and implying Chandler wouldn't be there voluntarily), and the punchline lands with the confidence of a room-killer. The quotability is high — this line gets pulled out of context and still works.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The candles are lit, the wine is chilled, there's moonlight streaming through the window...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, when is it ever going to be more perfect than this?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, I know, you're right.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what are you waiting for?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't know. What if she says no? What if the moment passes? What if—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What if? Ross, there is no 'what if.' This IS the moment. It doesn't get better than this. The candles, the wine, the moonlight... you think this happens every night?

jokes.text: Phoebe's weirdest place: 'Milwaukee.' She adds: 'It's a really weird place.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is answering 'weirdest place you've had sex' with specific, scandalous answers
jokes.punchline: Phoebe answers with a city, as if the location itself is the deviant element — and then earnestly defends it as 'a really weird place'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comic peak in the 'weirdest place' sequence. 'Milwaukee' as an answer is a perfectly absurdist non-sequitur that only Phoebe could deliver without irony. The follow-up defense — 'it's a really weird place' — makes it clear she is entirely sincere, which is funnier than any wink. Maximum character integration: this is 100% a Phoebe joke. The economy is flawless. One word does everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I need to tell you all something. I've been wanting to say this for a long time, and I just... I can't keep it inside anymore. Monica, Phoebe, Joey, what I'm about to tell you is—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Shh! Shh!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Shhhhh!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, be quiet!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? What's wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The game is on! Central Perk is about to announce the winner!

jokes.text: Ross: 'Disneyland, 1989. It's a small world after all.' [pause] 'The ride broke down, so Carol and I went behind those mechanical Dutch children. We were asked never to return to the Magic Kingdom.'
jokes.setup: Ross's answer to 'weirdest place you've had sex'
jokes.punchline: The collision of a wholesome Disney setting with the very specific detail of 'the mechanical Dutch children' as cover, capped by the formal consequence of being banned from the Magic Kingdom
jokes.explanation: A very strong joke with layered construction. The '1989' and 'It's a small world after all' are delivered like romantic nostalgia before the horror sets in. 'Behind those mechanical Dutch children' is a devastatingly specific detail — the more you picture it, the funnier it gets. 'We were asked never to return to the Magic Kingdom' has the dry, official language of a formal ban, which is the perfect close. Strong character integration: Ross having a documented history of inappropriate passion (later contrasted with his current passivity toward Rachel) is thematically rich.

dialogue.speaker: Jill
dialogue.line: Do you want some gum?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No thanks, I can't. Do you know how much sugar is in gum? It's like chewing a liquefied candy bar.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why did I say that? She was being nice. I should have just taken the gum. Now she thinks I'm weird.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Gum. It's just gum. It's not like she offered me a mangled animal carcass to chew on.

jokes.text: Rachel's 'weirdest place': '...the foot of the bed.' [long pause] 'Step back! We have a winner!'
jokes.setup: After Disneyland and Milwaukee, Rachel is pressured to share her most scandalous location
jokes.punchline: After elaborate buildup, Rachel's answer is the most domestic, boring, barely-counts answer possible — 'the foot of the bed'
jokes.explanation: The best punchline in the 'weirdest place' sequence and one of the episode's top moments. The joke is structurally brilliant: a long reluctance buildup, a dramatic pause, and then the most anticlimactic answer imaginable — followed by the group treating it as the unanimous winner. This works because of the character: Rachel's sheltered, controlled life with Barry is crystallized in one joke. The 'Step back! We have a winner!' reaction is the perfect ironic cherry on top. The structural patience here — making the audience wait — is professional-level writing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't believe I rejected the gum. What was I thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: At this point, I'd take anything from Jill. A piece of gum? Sure. A wrapper? Why not. A mangled animal carcass? Hand it over.

jokes.text: 'This must be what the fridge looks like with the door closed.' [pause] 'Spooky.'
jokes.setup: The group is sitting in the dark apartment during the blackout
jokes.punchline: Joey offers the profound observation that the dark apartment resembles the inside of a refrigerator — a thought that apparently disturbs him
jokes.explanation: A delightful Joey non-sequitur. The observation itself is technically correct but absurd to voice; the follow-up 'Spooky' implies Joey has genuinely unsettled himself with this thought. The food-as-reference-point is perfect Joey characterization. High character integration — only Joey's brain goes here.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: There was a blackout in New York City. This song's about how when we all work together, we can get through the worst of times. I stay away from dairy.

jokes.text: Someone opens the fridge and says: 'Anybody hungry? We got a Klondike... soup.'
jokes.setup: Joey's fridge observation leads someone to actually check the fridge
jokes.punchline: The Klondike bar has melted into soup — announced with the same casual cadence as any normal food offer
jokes.explanation: A clean situational joke with great economy. The mid-sentence pivot ('Klondike... soup') does the comedic work efficiently. The deadpan delivery amplifies it. A small but well-executed laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, so you told Rachel about Ross's party before me?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I didn't mean to! It just came out!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And now I know about it, which means I'm ahead of Monica in the information chain.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is so typical. I'm always the last to know everything.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Actually, wait. I just realized I didn't even know I had a crush on Joey until Chandler told me last week.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You have a crush on me?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So now you're second to last, and I'm third?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, you're second to last. I'm last on knowing about my own feelings.

jokes.text: Rachel explains Ross and Carol's Disneyland passion: 'It was the only thing to do that didn't have a line.'
jokes.setup: Rachel wistfully praises the kind of passion that would drive someone to have sex at Disneyland
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately undermines the romantic framing with a pragmatic, unromantic explanation — they did it because there was no queue
jokes.explanation: A sharp callback that punctures the romantic mythology Ross accidentally created. The specificity of 'the only thing without a line' is perfect — it reframes their passion as efficiency tourism. Good character integration: Ross's oblivious self-sabotage is consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, there's something I need to tell you. I've been wanting to say this for a long time and—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross, wait! Have you seen Mr. Whiskers? He got out of the apartment and I've been looking everywhere for him!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? No, I haven't seen— Monica, I really need to—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is a disaster! He's microchipped and he's up to date on his shots, but what if he's scared? What if he's in the rain? Oh God, we need to check the fire escape, and the basement, and—

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Barry wouldn't even kiss me on a miniature golf course. He said we held up the people behind us.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is contrasting her sheltered romantic life with the passionate Disneyland story
jokes.punchline: Barry's refusal to kiss on a mini golf course — citing the queue — makes him sound like the anti-romantic equivalent of a theme park efficiency manager
jokes.explanation: A good character joke that efficiently characterizes both Rachel (starved for romance) and Barry (a man who treats a kiss like an obstruction). The specific setting of miniature golf is well-chosen — already a low-romance venue, which makes Barry's anti-kiss stance doubly pathetic.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, a kitten! Everyone, look!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Aw, it's so scared. Here little guy, it's okay.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, we should sing to it. That'll make it feel better.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Um, Phoebe, I don't think that's—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: ♪ Little kitten, don't you fear... ♪

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: ♪ We are here, we are here... ♪

dialogue.speaker: All
dialogue.line: ♪ Little kitten, we will care for you... ♪

jokes.text: Ross philosophizes about passion burning out, concluding with 'But hopefully what you're left with is trust and security and...' — then: 'In my ex-wife's case, lesbianism.'
jokes.setup: Ross is delivering a sincere, slightly defensive speech about how passion gives way to deeper things in relationships
jokes.punchline: The speech collapses when he applies it to his own marriage — the thing that replaced passion in Carol's case was her coming out
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. Ross builds a sincere, slightly pompous romantic worldview speech — and then demolishes it with one word that reveals the specificity of his own painful situation. 'Lesbianism' as the punchline word is perfect: it's the most clinical possible term for the most personal possible revelation, delivered mid-philosophical-sentence. The structure is textbook: long sincere setup, sudden context collapse. This is extremely high character integration — this joke only exists because of Ross's specific backstory. Highly quotable out of context.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh no, what happened to you, sweetie? Don't worry, I'll fix you right up.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: There we go, a little of this hot wax and you'll be good as new.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, that's wax. You're waxing the cat.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? No, I'm not— Oh my God!

jokes.text: Chandler's confessional to camera (or to Joey on phone): 'It's never gonna happen.' — referring to Ross and Rachel.
jokes.setup: The Ross/Rachel dynamic has been building with Ross's romantic speech
jokes.punchline: Chandler delivers a flat, certain verdict on the show's central will-they-won't-they premise
jokes.explanation: A meta moment that's funnier in retrospect given how long the Ross/Rachel arc runs. In season 1 it works as character insight; on rewatch it's darkly funny dramatic irony. The flat certainty is good Chandler deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We should try to find the owner.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Or we could just leave it in the hall and let it get trampled.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah?

jokes.text: Chandler: 'You waited too long to make your move, and now you're in the friend zone.' Ross: 'I'm not in the zone.' Chandler: 'No, Ross. You're mayor of the zone.'
jokes.setup: Chandler tells Ross he's in the 'friend zone' with Rachel
jokes.punchline: Ross's denial is met with an escalation — not just in the zone, but democratically elected its chief executive
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most culturally significant moment — this exchange essentially coined 'friend zone' as a pop culture term. The escalation from 'in the zone' to 'mayor of the zone' is perfectly constructed. 'Mayor' implies permanence, community standing, and democratic legitimacy (he earned it). The quotability score is near-maximum because this line left the show and became part of the language. Strong structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I said 'perfection'? What was I thinking? 'Perfection'? That's not... I mean, who says that? That's not a word you use in a real conversation. I should have said 'nice' or 'great' or literally anything else. But no, I went with 'perfection' like some kind of idiot. I'm an idiot. A complete and total idiot.

jokes.text: Ross claims he's 'laying the groundwork' and getting 'closer every day' — Chandler interrupts with: 'Priesthood!'
jokes.setup: Ross insists he's making slow but deliberate progress toward asking Rachel out
jokes.punchline: Chandler's single-word interruption suggests the only destination for Ross's current trajectory is celibacy
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word does everything. Chandler doesn't need to explain; 'Priesthood' as a punchline word captures the entire critique of Ross's passivity (vow of celibacy, institutional commitment to avoiding the question). The structure is clean: Ross's meandering optimism, Chandler's single surgical word. Near-perfect economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So you're saying this is your kitten?

dialogue.speaker: Neighbor
dialogue.line: That's right. We've had her for months.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Then what's her name?

dialogue.speaker: Neighbor
dialogue.line: Uh... Fluffy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're lying. Watch this.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Come here, sweetie!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: She only responds to us. She doesn't know you at all.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're trying to steal our kitten! That's so messed up!

jokes.text: Ross: 'She just ran her fingers through my hair.' Chandler demonstrates the difference between 'running fingers through hair' and a 'tousle.'
jokes.setup: Ross interprets Rachel touching his hair as a romantic signal
jokes.punchline: Chandler physically demonstrates the distinction between a romantic hair-touch and a friendly tousle, proving Ross is misreading the signal
jokes.explanation: A good physical bit that pays off later when Rachel actually gives Ross 'a tousle' and Chandler gets to say 'that was no tousle.' The hair-touch taxonomy is an inventive way to dramatize Ross's delusional romantic reading of neutral signals. Rewatch value because of the payoff at 20:29.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So where's Paolo from?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Italy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Italy? No, I mean... tonight. Where's he coming tonight?

jokes.text: Chandler coaches Ross to go tell Rachel his feelings: 'What's messing you up? The wine? The moonlight?' — Ross is about to go, then everyone 'shushes' him because they hear something outside.
jokes.setup: Chandler finally gets Ross psyched up to make his move on Rachel
jokes.punchline: The moment is perfectly set up — then instantly derailed by the group shushing him to listen to something random outside
jokes.explanation: A functional comedic interrupt that serves the plot (introducing the cat that leads to Paolo). The joke is more structural than funny on its own — it's a narrative device dressed as a joke. Competent but not special.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That is funny. And Rachel keeps touching him.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know!

jokes.text: Jill offers Chandler gum. He asks: 'Is it sugarless?' She says no. He declines: 'Then no, thanks.' Internal: 'What was that? Mental note: If Jill Goodacre offers you gum, you take it. If she offers you mangled animal carcass, you take it!'
jokes.setup: Jill Goodacre makes the simple social gesture of offering Chandler gum
jokes.punchline: Chandler refuses on dietary grounds, then immediately realizes the catastrophic social error, escalating his self-instruction from 'take the gum' to 'take a mangled animal carcass'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is perfect cringe: Chandler, desperate to impress, reflexively rejects Jill's offer with the world's least charming concern ('is it sugarless?'). The internal escalation is the comedy: he correctly identifies the error immediately, then overcorrects into absurdism with 'mangled animal carcass.' The escalation from gum to carcass is the joke's engine, and the word 'mangled' is doing heavy lifting. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Watch this.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: *chokes and gags*

dialogue.speaker: Jill
dialogue.line: Are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: *continues choking*

jokes.text: Phoebe sings her blackout song: 'New York City has no power / And the milk is getting sour / But to me it is not scary / Because I stay away from dairy.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe improvises a song about the blackout
jokes.punchline: The song begins topically then takes a bizarre personal turn — her comfort with the blackout is specifically because she's dairy-free
jokes.explanation: A classic Phoebe song moment. The rhyme scheme is consistent (power/sour, scary/dairy) which gives it mock-professional polish, but the turn to her personal dietary habits as the crisis-management solution is pure Phoebe absurdism. 'I stay away from dairy' as a blackout coping mechanism is exactly the kind of specific non-sequitur that defines the character. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jill
dialogue.line: That was perfection.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah... yeah, it was.

jokes.text: Ross is about to tell Rachel his feelings. Joey blocks him: 'Where are you going? You can't go out there.' Ross: 'Why not?' Joey: 'Because of the reason.' Ross: 'That would be?' Joey: 'I can't tell you.'
jokes.setup: Ross is finally about to make his move on Rachel
jokes.punchline: Joey blocks him with the least convincing cover story in history — 'because of the reason' — then refuses to name the reason
jokes.explanation: A good Joey-logic joke. 'Because of the reason' is a perfect Joey explanation — it has the grammatical structure of a reason without any content. The escalating absurdity of him refusing to name the unnamed reason is funny. Strong character integration for Joey's particular brand of confidence-in-empty-statements.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, Rachel, I don't know what you're doing here. You're not like this.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, I just... I want to bite his lip.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, three seconds with Paolo and you're like weeks with Barry.

jokes.text: Joey tells Monica there's a surprise party for her. Monica is thrilled. Then it emerges Phoebe didn't know, and then Chandler didn't know — 'This is typical. I'm always the last to know.'
jokes.setup: Joey accidentally reveals Ross's 'surprise party' to Monica as cover for blocking her
jokes.punchline: The secret cascades — Monica knows, tells Phoebe, Phoebe wasn't told, and now Phoebe complains about always being last to know
jokes.explanation: A decent domino-fall structure joke. Each reveal undoes the previous person's advantage. The comedy is in the escalating incompetence of secret-keeping, but it doesn't land with particular force.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: P-Paolo, I... I think you should know that Rachel and I, we haven't... I mean, we haven't...

dialogue.speaker: Paolo
dialogue.line: Haven't what?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We haven't been together. That way. And I would be... I would be very sad if you hurt her.

dialogue.speaker: Paolo
dialogue.line: Very sad?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes. Very sad.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'I was the last to know when Chandler got bit by the peacock.' And: 'I was the last to know you had a crush on Joey.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is complaining about always being the last to find out things
jokes.punchline: Her examples include a peacock attack (absurd) and a Monica/Joey crush revelation (real)
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one line. 'Chandler got bit by the peacock' is a throwaway absurdist detail that implies a rich, unrevealed backstory — a Friends universe event we will never learn more about, which is funnier for its mystery. The Monica/Joey crush lands as a real revelation that triggers the next joke. The peacock detail earns high originality.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? You're a crap-weasel!

jokes.text: Monica had a crush on Joey. Joey: 'You had a crush on me?' Monica: 'All right, it wasn't a crush. It was a dent.' Joey, smugly: 'Big dent?'
jokes.setup: Monica tries to minimize her former crush on Joey by calling it a 'dent'
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately accepts the new terminology and uses it to fish for ego validation: 'Big dent?'
jokes.explanation: A sharp exchange. Monica's euphemism ('dent') is clever in itself, but Joey's instant adoption of it for his own vanity purposes ('big dent?') is the real joke. It's perfect Joey — completely unfazed by the diminishment, laser-focused on whether he still ranks high. Great character integration for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm ready. Start the countdown.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Five... four... three... two... one...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, what happens at zero?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's when we kiss, you idiot!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh! Okay, start again. I wasn't ready.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Five... four... three... two... one... zero...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Now?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes, NOW!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. Let's do this. Start the countdown again.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Five... four... three... two... one... zero... negative one... negative two...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't know! I got confused!

jokes.text: Monica explains the crush: 'You were moving your furniture. I thought you had nice arms.' Joey immediately: 'Nice arms, huh?' then flexes/shows off: 'Hey Mon, I'm moving the chair. Do anything for you?'
jokes.setup: Monica reluctantly explains the 'dent' was about Joey's arms while moving furniture
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately stages a repeat performance — pretending to move a chair in the dark — to see if the arms still work their magic
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Joey's response to 'I liked your arms' is to immediately market his arms again. The fake furniture move in a dark apartment, during a blackout, asking 'do anything for you?' is perfectly Joey — oblivious to the awkwardness, entirely self-promotional. 9.0 character integration because no other character would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hahahaha! Hahahaha!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross! My party!

jokes.text: After the Monica/Joey crush revelation, the group looks at the stars through the window in awkward post-revelation silence — Phoebe breaks it with her philosophical 'I have a question. Actually it's not so much a question, it's more of a general wondering... ment.'
jokes.setup: The group is sitting in charged silence after the crush revelation
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's attempted philosophical transition trails off into '...ment' — she can't even complete the word 'wonderment'
jokes.explanation: A lovely Phoebe character moment. She fumbles the word 'wonderment' by splitting it into 'wondering' + '...ment' — a very specific kind of verbal mistake that's perfectly Phoebe (she commits to the thought but loses the word mid-stream). The awkward pause before it adds to the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jill
dialogue.line: I had a great blackout.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, me too.

jokes.text: Ross is mid-declaration of feelings to Rachel — 'Well, for a while now, I've been wanting to...' — interrupted when they both notice a stray cat landing on the balcony: 'Look at that little kitty!'
jokes.setup: Ross is finally making his long-awaited emotional declaration to Rachel
jokes.punchline: The romantic moment is destroyed by a cat appearing on the balcony, which Rachel finds more interesting than whatever Ross was about to say
jokes.explanation: A solid comedic interrupt that also serves the plot (introducing Paolo). The comedy is in the deflation — Ross's big moment stolen by a cat. Rachel's complete pivot to the cat underlines how unaware she is of what Ross was about to say.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I get a copy of that tape?

jokes.text: Ross and Rachel try to treat the cat's scratch: 'All right, this is just Bactine. It won't hurt.' [applies it] 'Ow!' 'Sorry, that was wax.'
jokes.setup: Ross reassures Rachel the antiseptic won't hurt
jokes.punchline: It hurts — and the reason is that it was accidentally wax (a completely wrong product), not Bactine
jokes.explanation: A quick physical comedy beat. The structure is clean (promise of no pain → immediate pain → absurd explanation). 'That was wax' is a funny non-sequitur explanation that raises more questions than it answers. Efficient but not remarkable.

jokes.text: Monica argues the cat 'Tooty' shouldn't be put in the hall during a blackout: 'She'll get trampled.' Joey: 'Yeah?' [skeptical pause implying a cat cannot get trampled in a hallway]
jokes.setup: Monica insists it would be dangerous to put the cat in the hallway
jokes.punchline: Joey's dry 'yeah?' implies he's not buying the trampling scenario in a residential hallway
jokes.explanation: A small reaction beat. Not particularly inventive but functional — Joey's skepticism is appropriate and mildly funny. Below average for the episode.

jokes.text: Chandler internal: 'Damage control. Get back to the gum.' Then out loud: 'Gum would be perfection.'
jokes.setup: After fumbling the gum offer, Chandler decides to circle back and accept it
jokes.punchline: His attempt to recover produces an even worse line: 'gum would be perfection' — elevating gum to a philosophical ideal
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's funniest single moment and one of the best Chandler jokes in the series. The setup is Chandler's damage-control attempt; the punchline is that his recovery is worse than the original error. 'Gum would be nice' would have been fine. 'Gum would be great' would have been acceptable. 'Gum would be perfection' is an Aristotelian declaration that gum represents the pinnacle of human achievement — said to someone offering him Juicy Fruit. The escalation from mistake to worse mistake is textbook cringe comedy, and the word 'perfection' is doing extraordinary work. Near-maximum quotability.

jokes.text: Chandler's internal reaction: 'Gum would be perfection? Could've said gum would be nice. But no. For me, gum is perfection. I loathe myself!'
jokes.setup: Chandler immediately recognizes 'gum would be perfection' was wrong
jokes.punchline: 'I loathe myself!' — the internal verdict is total self-condemnation
jokes.explanation: The immediate callback that turns the knife. The internal monologue maps the exact slide from 'nice' (fine) to 'perfection' (catastrophic), landing on 'I loathe myself' — which is funny in its totality of self-judgment over gum etiquette. The self-awareness that makes it worse ('Could've said gum would be nice') is sharp writing. Together with #46, this is the episode's comedic centerpiece.

jokes.text: Ross and Rachel try to find the cat's owner. They knock on a door; Joey says of the neighbor: 'Oh no, they're nuns. They hate all living things.'
jokes.setup: They need to knock on doors to find the cat's owner
jokes.punchline: Joey identifies some neighbors as nuns and characterizes them as universally misanthropic ('they hate all living things')
jokes.explanation: A funny throwaway line. The joke is in the absurdity of Joey's specific knowledge of his neighbors' theological status AND their personality ('they hate all living things') — as if these are known facts about the building. Lightly subversive and very Joey.

jokes.text: The man who claims the cat: Ross/Joey asks 'He seems to hate you. Are you sure?' Man: 'It's my cat. Give me my cat.' Then: 'What's his name?' — 'Bob Buttons.' The cat ignores 'Bob Buttons.'
jokes.setup: A man claims the cat is his; the cat's hostility toward him raises suspicion
jokes.punchline: 'Bob Buttons' is such an implausible cat name — and the cat doesn't respond — that everyone (and the audience) doubts his ownership
jokes.explanation: A solid small-character bit. 'Bob Buttons' is a funny cat name because it's so specifically wrong — too formal, too alliterative, and the cat's utter indifference to it confirms the lie. The 'he seems to hate you' challenge is a nice setup.

jokes.text: After the cat scratches the fake owner: 'You are a very bad man!' / 'You owe me a cat.'
jokes.setup: The fake cat owner is exposed when the cat attacks him
jokes.punchline: 'You owe me a cat' — as if demanding restitution for a cat they found five minutes ago
jokes.explanation: A functional tag to the Bob Buttons scene. 'You owe me a cat' is a funny non-sequitur demand — they had no ownership of the cat — but it's delivered with the confidence of a legal claim. Mildly funny.

jokes.text: Joey, upon seeing Paolo: 'Mon, wanna go for a ride in my racecar? I'll bring my arms. We can bring my wheelbarrow for your teeth!'
jokes.setup: Paolo appears and is clearly devastatingly handsome; the men in the group react
jokes.punchline: Joey's competitive response is to immediately try to sell Monica on his own physical attributes — arms, racecar — in the face of superior competition, then throws in the 'wheelbarrow for teeth' jab
jokes.explanation: A callback that doesn't land as well as the original. The racecar joke is underwritten and the wheelbarrow callback feels recycled rather than earned. Joey's competitive vanity is in-character but the execution is a bit scattered.

jokes.text: Rachel cheerfully: 'That cat turned out to be Paolo's cat. Isn't that funny?' Ross, barely containing himself: 'That IS funny. And Rachel keeps touching him.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is delighted by the coincidence of the cat leading her to Paolo
jokes.punchline: Ross's 'that IS funny' is barely controlled sarcasm — he's watching his romantic moment evaporate while Rachel is thrilled
jokes.explanation: A good reaction beat for Ross. The 'that IS funny' caps his barely-concealed anguish, and 'Rachel keeps touching him' is delivered as a wounded observation. The comedy is in the gap between Rachel's delight and Ross's misery.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'I looked all over and couldn't find the kitty anywhere.' Monica: 'I found him. It was Paolo's cat.' Phoebe: 'Well, there you go. Last to know again.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been left out of the Paolo cat revelation loop
jokes.punchline: She applies her 'last to know' complaint to even this trivial development, with resigned acceptance
jokes.explanation: A solid running gag callback. The joke is in Phoebe treating a cat's ownership as the same category as Chandler's peacock attack. The resigned 'well, there you go' is a nice touch — she's accepted this as her fate.

jokes.text: Phoebe meets Paolo: 'You betcha!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is introduced to the devastatingly handsome Italian Paolo
jokes.punchline: 'You betcha!' — a wildly inappropriate/incongruous response to being introduced to a stranger, suggesting enthusiastic endorsement of his existence
jokes.explanation: A small but delightful Phoebe moment. 'You betcha!' in response to being introduced to someone makes no grammatical sense as a greeting — which is what makes it perfectly Phoebe. Maximum economy (two words), high character integration.

jokes.text: Chandler's friend on the phone coaches him: 'Blow a bubble. A bubble's good. It's got a boyish charm. It's impish.' Chandler tries — and the gum bubble goes catastrophically wrong.
jokes.setup: Chandler is being coached via phone on how to seem charming while chewing the gum; blowing a bubble is proposed as 'impish'
jokes.punchline: The bubble presumably pops on his face in a mortifying way
jokes.explanation: Good escalation in the gum subplot. The coaching language ('impish') is itself funny — 'impish' is not a quality one strategically deploys. The physical fail is well-earned by the over-thought setup. Part of the sustained Chandler/Jill comedic arc.

jokes.text: 'Nice going, imp!' then Chandler tries to put the popped gum back in his mouth: 'All I need to do is reach over and put it back in my mouth.' Internal: 'Good save! We're back on track and I'm... chewing someone else's gum.'
jokes.setup: The bubble fails; Chandler decides to retrieve the gum
jokes.punchline: He accidentally picks up Jill's discarded gum and is now chewing it — a new horror discovered mid-chew
jokes.explanation: Excellent sustained cringe escalation. 'Good save! We're back on track and I'm...' creates a false relief before the horror of 'chewing someone else's gum.' The internal optimism collapsing in real time is a great comedic structure. The Chandler ATM subplot has been the episode's best-sustained running bit.

jokes.text: Chandler's reaction to chewing Jill's gum: 'This is not my gum! Oh my God! Oh my God!' — then begins choking on it.
jokes.setup: Chandler has been chewing Jill Goodacre's discarded gum
jokes.punchline: His panic causes him to choke, making the situation even worse — and now Jill has to save him
jokes.explanation: The escalation peak of the Chandler/Jill subplot. Every attempt to recover makes things worse. Choking on the gum is the physical crescendo that forces Jill to intervene — which is both the worst and best possible outcome for Chandler.

jokes.text: After Jill saves Chandler from choking, he says 'That was... that was...' and she finishes: 'Perfection?'
jokes.setup: Chandler is searching for words after being saved by Jill
jokes.punchline: Jill completes his sentence with 'Perfection?' — a direct callback to 'gum would be perfection,' which she apparently found endearing enough to remember
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. A perfect callback structure: 'gum would be perfection' was Chandler's most embarrassing moment, but Jill has clearly found it charming — she returns it to him as a gift when he's searching for words. The word 'perfection' has now completed a full journey from embarrassing overstatement to mutual joke to tender moment. The economy is perfect (one word), the structure is textbook callback closure, and the character integration is high — only this sequence of events could produce this moment. This approaches the level of a truly memorable sitcom beat.

jokes.text: Ross watches Rachel touch Paolo's hair — Chandler, who explained 'running fingers through hair' vs. 'tousle' earlier, says: 'That was no tousle.'
jokes.setup: Chandler earlier defined the distinction between romantic and friendly hair-touching to Ross
jokes.punchline: Watching Rachel run her fingers through Paolo's hair, Chandler confirms with understated finality that this is the romantic kind
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback with near-perfect structure. Earlier Chandler established the taxonomy (running fingers through hair = romantic, tousle = friendly). Now, watching Rachel with Paolo, the taxonomy is applied with devastating precision: 'That was no tousle' confirms Ross's worst fear in four words. The economy is outstanding — the callback does all the work. This is great comedy writing: patience, payoff, and character consequence all in one line.

jokes.text: The group watches Rachel interact with Paolo, who says something. Monica/Phoebe: 'What'd he say that was so funny?' Rachel: 'I have absolutely no idea.' Monica: 'That's classic.'
jokes.setup: Paolo says something in Italian that makes Rachel laugh
jokes.punchline: Rachel has no idea what he said — she's laughing at pure charm with zero content — and Monica calls this 'classic'
jokes.explanation: A sharp observational joke about the nature of attraction — Rachel finds Paolo's unknown Italian words hilarious simply because he's beautiful. Monica's 'that's classic' endorsement is both sincere and a commentary on all of their standards. Clean and knowing.

jokes.text: Rachel's confessional: 'My God, you guys! What am I doing? This is so un-me!' Joey: 'If you want, I'll do it.'
jokes.setup: Rachel expresses guilty excitement about Paolo being superficial and language-barrier-limited
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately volunteers to pursue Paolo on her behalf — or perhaps to pursue Paolo himself
jokes.explanation: A quick character joke. 'If you want, I'll do it' is ambiguous in a funny way — is Joey offering to pursue Paolo, or pursue Rachel's impulse on her behalf? The ambiguity is probably intentional. Good economy.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'I just wanna bite his bottom lip. But I won't.' Beat. 'The first time he smiled at me, those seconds were more exciting than weeks with Barry.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is confessing her attraction to Paolo and processing her own feelings
jokes.punchline: The specific metric — seconds with Paolo > weeks with Barry — quantifies the failure of her former engagement with surgical precision
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp line. The 'seconds vs. weeks' ratio is a precise, funny way to eulogize a failed engagement. The setup ('I just wanna bite his bottom lip. But I won't.') is also funny in its self-restraint — she's decided to not bite. Good character writing for Rachel.

jokes.text: Someone asks Rachel if she and Paolo 'rented mopeds' — Rachel redirects: 'Because I've heard... Oh, it's not about that right now.'
jokes.setup: Conversation drifts toward the practical (mopeds) while Rachel is in full romantic reverie
jokes.punchline: The moped tangent is real enough to get partially into the conversation before Rachel shuts it down — implying they may well have discussed mopeds
jokes.explanation: A minor background joke. The moped reference is slightly confusing out of context (they presumably mimed/gestured about mopeds with Paolo) and the comedic payoff is small. Below-average for this episode.

jokes.text: Ross confronts Paolo: 'Rachel and I are... we're kind of a thing.' Paolo: 'Thing?' Ross: 'Thing. Yes, thing.' Paolo: 'You have the sex?' Ross: 'No. No, technically the sex is not being had.'
jokes.setup: Ross tries to assert a relationship with Rachel to Paolo using minimal shared vocabulary
jokes.punchline: Paolo cuts through Ross's euphemisms with direct broken-English inquiry: 'You have the sex?' — forcing Ross into a hilarious bureaucratic denial
jokes.explanation: An excellent cross-cultural cringe comedy exchange. Paolo's ESL phrasing ('You have the sex?') is both linguistically funny and cuts through Ross's diplomatic evasiveness. Ross's response — 'No. No, technically the sex is not being had' — is a masterpiece of passive-voice denial. The legalistic 'technically the sex is not being had' makes it sound like a formal inquiry. High character integration: only Ross would respond to 'you have the sex?' with passive-voice grammar.

jokes.text: Ross tells Paolo 'Rachel and I should be together. And if you get in the... in bed...' — catches himself — 'No, not where I was going. If you get in the way of us becoming a thing... I would be, well, very sad.'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to deliver a firm warning to Paolo about Rachel
jokes.punchline: His warning accidentally steers toward 'in bed' before he corrects himself, and his ultimate threat is that he'd be 'very sad' — the most pathetically understated warning possible
jokes.explanation: A strong character moment. The accidental 'in bed' slip is a nice quick beat, but the real joke is Ross's threat: 'I would be, well, very sad.' As romantic rival warnings go, this is the most Ross thing possible — not anger, not dominance, just personal sadness. Perfect character integration.

jokes.text: Ross asks if Paolo understands, implying he might not know any English. Paolo: 'Little.' Ross: 'Do you know the word crap-weasel?' Paolo: 'No.' Ross: 'That's funny. You are a huge crap-weasel.'
jokes.setup: Ross discovers Paolo understands some English; he tests the extent with a made-up insult
jokes.punchline: 'Crap-weasel' as a custom insult — checking if Paolo knows it before deploying it — is a roundabout way to call someone a name they won't understand
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The logic is gloriously Ross: he wants to insult Paolo but needs to confirm Paolo won't understand the insult. So he asks if he knows 'crap-weasel' — tipping off Paolo to the insult — then delivers it anyway. 'Crap-weasel' as a compound insult is an inspired coinage; it's specific, evocative, and absurd in exactly the right way. 'You are a HUGE crap-weasel' — the addition of 'huge' — is the perfect emphasis. This joke is highly quotable and holds up as one of Ross's funniest moments in the series.

jokes.text: Monica teaches Paolo to snap his fingers. His attempts are completely unsuccessful; she coaches: 'You gotta whip it.' — the lesson continues as completely inept for an extended beat.
jokes.setup: Monica tries to teach Paolo to snap his fingers (apparently the group needs him to do something)
jokes.punchline: Paolo simply cannot snap — the simple coordination required is entirely beyond him — which Monica addresses with the earnest instruction 'you gotta whip it'
jokes.explanation: A physical comedy beat that's funnier as a performance than on the page. The joke is in the execution — a beautiful Italian man who can't snap — but there's not much craft here. Relies entirely on Paolo's performance.

jokes.text: The last candle countdown: 'Ten, nine, eight, seven... minus 46, minus 47, minus 48...'
jokes.setup: The group counts down as the last candle is about to go out
jokes.punchline: After 'seven,' the count jumps to negative numbers — someone is counting backward from somewhere with no mathematical logic
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist gag. The sudden jump to negative numbers is mildly funny — someone in the group clearly doesn't understand how countdowns work. A brief, light laugh. Not especially crafted but amiable.

jokes.text: Joey tells Ross about the 'surprise party' for Monica being found out: 'This has been fun.' Then, extremely awkwardly, tries to remind Ross he needs to throw Monica's party.
jokes.setup: Joey accidentally revealed the surprise party; now he has to somehow prompt Ross to still throw it
jokes.punchline: Joey's attempt to course-correct is maximally awkward — pretending nothing happened while passing on party-planning responsibility
jokes.explanation: A weak tag on the surprise party storyline. The comedy potential of Joey's situational incompetence isn't fully exploited here. Functional plot resolution but modest laughs.

jokes.text: Jill Goodacre says goodbye to Chandler: 'Thanks for letting me use your phone and for saving my life. Well, goodbye, Chandler. I had a great blackout.'
jokes.setup: The blackout ends; Jill and Chandler say goodbye
jokes.punchline: 'I had a great blackout' — said with sincere warmth, as if 'blackout' is a social event one has or doesn't have
jokes.explanation: A warm, satisfying button on the Chandler/Jill subplot. 'I had a great blackout' works because it treats a citywide emergency as a social occasion — which, for these two, it essentially was. The callback to 'perfection' having worked is implied. A good closing beat.

jokes.text: Chandler, to the empty ATM vestibule after Jill leaves: 'Hi, I'm account number 7143457. I don't know if you got that, but I would really like a copy of the tape.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is left alone in the ATM vestibule; there's a security camera
jokes.punchline: He introduces himself by account number to the security camera and formally requests a copy of the tape — as a souvenir of his time with Jill
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and a near-perfect button. Chandler addressing the security camera by account number — adopting the formal language of a banking transaction to request a personal keepsake — is conceptually brilliant. It's completely in character (deflecting vulnerability with bureaucratic humor), the premise is original (I've never seen this joke before), and the specificity of the account number makes it funnier than a generic request would be. This is the kind of final joke that sends audiences out happy. High on all craft dimensions.

jokes.text: Final scene: Chandler calls the ATM (or bank): 'Hi, I'm account number 7143457. I don't know if you got that, but I would really like a copy of the tape.'
jokes.setup: Chandler's entire bumbling encounter with Jill Goodacre was presumably caught on ATM security camera
jokes.punchline: He wants a copy of the tape — to memorialize it, presumably because despite the humiliation, Jill Goodacre said goodbye to him by name
jokes.explanation: Perfect closing joke for the episode. Chandler identifying himself by account number to a security camera, requesting a copy of his own humiliating tape, is both absurd and deeply in character. The joke reframes his entire disaster as something he'd treasure — and it's a funny beat that closes the ATM storyline with genuine wit. The account number delivery ('I don't know if you got that') is the right touch of self-awareness.

tmdb_overview: A power outage leaves Chandler stranded in an ATM vestibule with Victoria's Secret model Jill Goodacre, whom he desperately tries to impress, Ross tries to ask Rachel out on a date, and Joey learns that Monica used to be infatuated with him.
insight: Blackout setting enables 41 jokes in 23 minutes—Friends' densest premiere-season episode.
